checks: A finite Borel measure has upper semicontinuous closed-halfspace depth: expand any closed cap of mass below a threshold to put a contained mark in its interior, and use continuity from above. This justifies the attained fiber maxima on each compact body at every parameter, including measures with pure-base boundary mass.

A circuit selected at a deepest base has old raw mass Q and interior anchor, so its root exists and tends to Q. Any supplied circuit at a nondeep base tends to its own old mass q_z below Q. Finitely many choices in a fixed selection share a neighborhood.

At a nondeep mark its depth is below Q, so some old closed containing cap already has mass below Q. If its normal is pure-base, reanchor at the mark and choose a nonzero continuous component small enough to preserve all strict exclusions of the old cap. Each excluded base has strictly negative base margin at the reanchored threshold, and finite bounded old fibers give a common perturbation size. An included old base could contribute at most its whole old mass, so the tilted cap costs no more than the old cap.

For any such nonvertical cap the cap mass is continuous in threshold because its level sets have zero fiber volume. Relax the threshold to put the mark in the cap interior while keeping strict slack. A finite subcover of the old compact fiber covers a neighborhood of it in the base plane and hence also the new fiber for small Hausdorff displacement. These fixed cap masses remain continuous in p by the same shape estimate, so the finite slack gap is uniform after shrinking.

A mark on each deepest site is bounded by its exact root, and a mark on any nondeep site by a cap of mass below the largest deepest root. Dividing the pointwise inequality by positive M(p) gives the global inequality. All roots at old deepest sites equal Q, so equality holds at p_0. The proof fixes an arbitrary circuit selection and makes no uniformity claim over all selections.
